verdict.rationale: The phrase chilia ete (G5507 plus G2094, a thousand years) appears as a defined unit only in Revelation 20:2-7, six times across six verses, and nowhere else in either Testament. The verb ezesan (aorist of zao G2198, they lived or came to life) is used for one group on thrones in 20:4 and again of the rest of the dead in 20:5, with anastasis he prote (G0386, the first resurrection) as the lexical hinge. Three readings are defensible from the words: a sequential reading takes ezesan in one bodily sense both times and places Christ's return (chapter 19) before the reign; a non-bodily reading takes the souls (psychas) of 20:4 as enthroned regenerate or martyred saints and chilia ete as a symbolic span of the present age; a triumphalist reading takes chilia ete as a long figurative gospel epoch culminating in the return. The Greek of Revelation 20 nowhere uses parousia or any return-vocabulary at the start of the thousand years, and the wider canon supplies symbolic numerics (Rev 11:3, 12:6, 14:20; 2 Pet 3:8) on the one hand and concrete day-of-the-LORD imagery (Zech 14; Isa 11; 65) on the other without ranking them. The verdict held is therefore disputed at the lexical level, on the same footing as amillennialism.

scripture.force: An angel binds (edesen, aorist of deo G1210) the dragon, who is named the ancient serpent and the devil and Satan, for chilia ete (G5507 plus G2094, a thousand years). This is the first of six occurrences of the bounded phrase chilia ete in 20:2-7, and the only place in the canon where the phrase is a defined block. The verb deo is the same verb used of binding the strong man in Matthew 12:29 and Mark 3:27, which is the lexical link by which a non-future reading takes Satan's binding as already accomplished in Christ's first-advent ministry rather than as a future epoch.

Satan is cast into the abyss (abyssos G0012) and sealed so that he will not deceive (planao G4105) the nations until the chilia ete are completed (telesthe, aorist passive of teleo). The verb planao is used pan-canonically of eschatological deception (Matt 24:4-5, 24; 2 Tim 3:13; Rev 12:9; 13:14; 19:20). Whether the present age is one in which Satan is bound from totally deceiving the nations or not is the precise point on which lexical data is genuinely silent, since the sealing clause states only the duration and the purpose, not the absolute extent of restriction.

John sees thrones and souls (psychas) of those beheaded for the testimony of Jesus, and ezesan (aorist of zao G2198) plus ebasileusan (aorist of basileuo G0936) with Christ chilia ete. The verb zao occurs 143 times in the Greek NT and carries both bodily senses (John 11:25; Rev 1:18 of Christ alive after death) and non-bodily senses (Rom 6:11 alive to God; Gal 2:20; Heb 12:9). The explicit grammatical subject is psychas (souls), which a non-bodily reading takes as decisive against physical resurrection here and a literal reading explains as a synecdoche for whole persons. Neither grammar alone nor the noun psychas alone forecloses the other reading.

The rest of the dead did not live (ouk ezesan, same verb as v.4) until the chilia ete were completed. This is the anastasis he prote (G0386, the first resurrection). The lexical hinge is whether the identical verb ezesan bears the same sense in both clauses. If it does (the standard lexical principle of consistent sense within an adjacent parallel), the second group's coming-to-life is bodily, which forces the first group's to be bodily as well, yielding two bodily resurrections. If verse 4 is non-bodily and verse 5 is bodily, the parallel is broken by an unstated shift. The label anastasis he prote distinguishes a first from a second, which the pan-canonical use of anastasis (42 occurrences, dominantly bodily: John 11:24; Acts 4:33; 1 Cor 15) inclines toward a bodily reading, but the Revelation context permits a figurative one.

Blessed and holy is the one having part in the first resurrection (anastasis G0386), over whom the second death has no authority; they will be priests of God and of Christ and basileusousin (future of basileuo G0936) with him chilia ete. The pairing of first resurrection with escape from the second death is read by a future-bodily lens as marking a raised company before a later judgment, and by a present-spiritual lens as the regenerate soul secure in the intermediate state. The clause does not name the parousia and does not lexically locate Christ's return at the start of the thousand years.

When the chilia ete are completed, Satan will be released (luthesetai, future of luo G3089) from his prison. The verb luo is the lexical inverse of edesen (G1210) in 20:2; binding and loosing frame the thousand-year block as a bounded interval. The verbs themselves are ordinary lexical items and do not specify whether the interval is a literal millennium or a symbolic span.

With the Lord one day is as chilia ete and chilia ete as one day. This is the only place outside Revelation 20 where the bounded phrase chilia ete appears, and it appears explicitly as a symbolic equivalence with one day (hos hemera mia, with the particle hos signaling figurative comparison). The verse does not say the Revelation 20 thousand years is symbolic, but it shows the same vocabulary used elsewhere by an apostle in an explicitly symbolic way, which is the lexical warrant for the non-literal reading.

The two witnesses prophesy chilias diakosias hexekonta hemeras (a thousand two hundred sixty days). Three other Revelation uses of chilioi (here, 12:6, 14:20) appear in compound numbers that are widely taken as symbolic time spans or symbolic measures. This shows that Revelation itself uses chilioi within figurative numerical schemes, which is the in-book lexical warrant for reading chilia ete in 20:2-7 symbolically rather than literally.

His feet shall stand (amad H5975) on the Mount of Olives, which splits, chatsi (H2677, half) toward east and chatsi toward west. The text describes a theophanic day of the LORD with concrete topography but assigns no thousand-year duration and gives no sequence relative to any resurrection. The half-and-half splitting (chatsi) is geographic, not temporal, so it cannot by itself supply a millennial timetable.

The LORD shall be (hayah H1961) king (melek H4428) over all the earth, the LORD one (echad H0259) and his name one. This universal kingship is lexically open as to whether it denotes a discrete future earthly reign of fixed length or the consummated reign of God without a thousand-year interim. The verse supplies kingship but not chronology.

The wolf (zeeb H2061) shall dwell (gur H1481) with the lamb (kebes H3532), describing a pacified order. The imagery is read by a future-earthly view as conditions of a coming earthly reign and by a realized view as the redeemed order inaugurated in Christ. The vocabulary is descriptive of harmony, not of a thousand-year span, so it neither dates nor demands a literal millennium.

No more shall there be in it an infant that lives only a few days, nor an old man who does not fill out his days, for the youth shall die (mut H4191) a hundred years old (shanah H8141). The text pictures an era in which death (mut) is still present yet abnormal, which a future-earthly reading takes as a key lexical anchor: it cannot be the new heavens and new earth of Revelation 21:4 where death is no more, so it must denote an intervening era. A figurative reading takes the vocabulary as hyperbolic blessing imagery for the new creation itself. The presence of mut in the eschatological vision is the lexical pressure point.

The disciples ask whether at this time he will restore (apokathistemi G0600) the kingdom to Israel. The verb apokathistemi denotes restoration to a former state. Christ's reply in v.7 redirects to times and seasons hidden in the Father's authority without denying the category of the question. The literal reading takes the unrebuked question as preserving the expectation of an earthly Israel-centered restoration that the post-parousia thousand years answers. A non-literal reading takes the kingdom restoration as fulfilled in the Spirit-empowered church (v.8). The verb itself is lexically neutral on chronology.

Each in his own order (idios tagma G5001): Christ the firstfruits, then those who are Christ's at his coming (en te parousia, G3952). The noun tagma is a hapax in the NT (one occurrence) and means rank or order. Paul names two ranks, Christ then his people, both tied to the parousia. The lexical question is whether tagma admits more ranks (a third group after a gap, hence a future earthly era between Christ's people and the end) or only the two named. Paul's wording does not lexically exclude a further rank but does not name one either, so the text is genuinely underdetermined on this point.

All who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come forth, those who did good to an anastasis of life (anastasis zoes) and those who did evil to an anastasis of judgment (anastasis kriseos). The single sentence describes a single hour (v.28) with two outcomes within one resurrection event named anastasis. This is the single-resurrection pattern in lexically explicit form. The literal reading of Revelation 20 must reconcile this single hour with two resurrections separated by chilia ete, either by treating John's hour as compressed prophetic language or by reading the second outcome as the second-stage resurrection. The texts together are not flatly contradictory but they are also not flatly harmonized at the word level.

complicating_texts.resolution: The single verb ezesan (G2198) governs both the company of v.4 and the rest of the dead in v.5. A sequential reading insists the verb cannot shift sense within two adjacent clauses, so both denote bodily coming-to-life, yielding two resurrections separated by chilia ete and a future reign. A non-bodily reading observes that v.4 names the subjects as psychas (souls) and sets the action among heavenly thrones, permitting a different sense for the first group (entrance into heavenly life or enthronement) while the second group's clause concerns physical raising at the end. Lexicography does not adjudicate the parallel principle versus the noun-psychas restriction, so the complication is recognized as genuinely unresolved at the word level and drives the disputed verdict rather than being dissolved by it.

The noun psychas (souls) as the explicit subject of ezesan is the chief complication for a straightforward bodily reading. If souls are the ones who lived and reigned, the coming-to-life may describe disembodied life or enthronement rather than physical resurrection, undercutting a clean two-bodily-resurrection scheme. The literal reading answers that psychas can stand for whole persons by synecdoche and that the following reign vocabulary presupposes embodiment. Both moves are lexically permissible. The complication is acknowledged but cannot be lexically dissolved.

Christ teaches a single hour in which all in the tombs hear his voice and come forth to two destinies, anastasis zoes and anastasis kriseos. This single-event two-outcome pattern is the textually clearest NT resurrection schema and uses the same noun (anastasis G0386) Revelation 20 uses. A literal Revelation 20 reading must say John 5 collapses a temporally separated pair into a prophetic horizon, or that the second outcome there is the same as the second resurrection of Rev 20:5. The reconciliation is possible but is not on the surface of either text. Recorded here as addressed but unresolved at the word level.

Paul orders the resurrection as Christ the firstfruits, then those who are Christ's at his parousia (G3952), and then the end (telos, v.24). The vocabulary names two tagma (G5001, a hapax) plus a final consummation. The text does not name a third tagma between parousia and end, which is the lexical pressure against a separate post-parousia millennial era containing additional events. A literal-millennium reading takes the chilia ete to fall inside the implied gap between v.23's parousia and v.24's telos; a non-millennial reading takes parousia and telos as the same event. Lexically the text is silent on which.

Isaiah's vision contains the verb mut (H4191, die) in the eschatological state, which is incompatible with the Revelation 21:4 promise that there will be no more death. A future-earthly reading uses this incompatibility as a lexical wedge for an intervening era still touched by mortality (the millennium). A figurative reading takes the language as hyperbolic blessing imagery within new-creation discourse rather than a literal description of conditions. The wedge is lexically real but does not by itself name the duration of any intervening era.

Peter explicitly uses chilia ete in a symbolic equivalence: with the Lord one day is as chilia ete and chilia ete as one day. The particle hos (as) marks the comparison as figurative. This is the only non-Revelation use of the bounded phrase in the canon, and it shows the same vocabulary functioning symbolically in apostolic teaching. A literal-millennium reading replies that one symbolic use elsewhere does not force a symbolic use here, especially since 2 Peter is comparing temporal scale generally; a non-literal reading replies that the apostolic precedent shows the phrase carries no automatic literal sense. Addressed; lexically underdetermined.

variants.note: Revelation is outside the CBGM 3 John sample, so no ECM-published apparatus was consulted. The Nestle-Aland sigla visible in the supplied Greek of Revelation 20 mark minor word-order and morphological variants around chilia ete, ezesan, and the verbs of binding and loosing; none of them shifts the lexical pressure point of whether ezesan means bodily resurrection or whether chilia ete is literal. The verdict does not turn on any variant unit.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads the chronological flow of Revelation 19 to 20 as sequential: Christ returns on the white horse in chapter 19, then in chapter 20 Satan is bound and the chilia ete begin. Takes both occurrences of ezesan (G2198) in 20:4-5 in the same bodily sense, so anastasis he prote (G0386) is the bodily raising of the saints before chilia ete and the rest are raised bodily after, with basileuo (G0936) a real reign. Adds the lexical pressure of Isa 65:20 (death still present), Acts 1:6 (restoration to Israel not denied), and the unrebuked disciple question for an intervening earthly era. The position is strongest where it lets the standard sense of bodily-resurrection vocabulary stand in the most explicit millennial passage.

Takes ezesan in v.4 as the heavenly life or enthronement of souls (psychas explicit subject) and the first resurrection as regeneration or the saints' entry into the intermediate state, with chilia ete as a symbolic figure for the entire interadvent age. Cites the symbolic numerics across Revelation (Rev 11:3, 12:6, 14:20) and the explicit symbolic use of chilia ete in 2 Pet 3:8, the single-resurrection pattern of John 5:28-29 (one hour, two destinies under one anastasis), and the absence of parousia vocabulary in Revelation 20. On this reading there is no future post-parousia earthly millennium and Christ returns once to the final judgment. The position is strongest where it lets the consistent NT pattern of one parousia and one bodily resurrection event control the figurative numerics of an apocalyptic chapter.

Treats chilia ete as a long symbolic period of gospel triumph within history that precedes Christ's return, so Christ comes after, not before, the thousand-year flourishing. The verbs basileuo and ezesan are read as the spiritual reign of the saints expanding in the present age, with Satan bound from preventing the gospel's progress to the nations. Cites the Matthew 12:29 binding of the strong man (deo G1210) as already accomplished in Christ. The position is strongest where it lets the kingdom growth motifs of the Gospels and the worldwide vocabulary of the Great Commission control the timing of the parousia.

hermeneutics.notes: The dispute is structural and lexical at once. The decisive question is whether the single verb ezesan carries one sense across Revelation 20:4-5 and whether chilia ete is literal or symbolic. Revelation's own pattern of symbolic numerics (1260 days, 144000, the sevens) sits alongside the chronological flow of chapters 19 to 20 that reads naturally as sequential. The OT anchors (Zechariah 14, Isaiah 11, Isaiah 65, Romans 11) supply kingship and restoration vocabulary and one explicit anomaly (death in Isa 65:20) but no chronology that fixes a return before a thousand-year span. Analogia scripturae yields the symbolic 2 Pet 3:8 use of chilia ete on one side and the single-resurrection John 5:28-29 pattern on one side, against the natural sequential reading of Rev 19-20 on the other. The lexicon does not break the tie.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: The relationship between the return of Christ, a thousand-year reign, and the present age, as that relationship is expressed in Revelation 20:1-7 and related texts.
stem_audit.notes: The original stem encodes a premillennial sequence by asserting Christ returns before a literal thousand-year reign that is future and distinct from the present age. That phrasing presupposes a literal reading of chilia ete and a particular ordering of the parousia relative to the millennium, which are the very points in dispute. The verdict is derived on the original stem; the neutralized form is recorded so the lexical contest, whether the thousand years is literal and whether the return precedes it, is visible without the wording prejudging it. Held to disputed at low confidence, the same lexical footing as the amillennialism and postmillennialism judgments, because the words underdetermine the millennial scheme.

lay_summary: This proposition stands or falls almost entirely on six verses, Revelation 20:1-7, with supporting glances at Zechariah 14, Isaiah 11, Isaiah 65, Romans 11, and Acts 1. The Greek phrase chilia ete, a thousand years, is a defined unit only in those six verses of Revelation 20, and apart from one passage in 2 Peter where it is used in a deliberately figurative way (one day as a thousand years), the phrase does not appear in the rest of the canon. So the entire millennial scheme rests on one apocalyptic block. Inside that block, two things have to be decided from the words on the page. First, the verb ezesan, they lived or they came to life, appears once for a group on thrones in verse 4 and again for the rest of the dead in verse 5. One reading holds that the same verb means the same thing both times, namely a bodily raising, so there are two bodily resurrections separated by a thousand years, which is named the first resurrection. On that reading the return of the King comes first and a real earthly reign follows. A second reading notes that the ones who come to life in verse 4 are called souls and are pictured among heavenly thrones, which allows that first coming-to-life to mean entrance into heavenly life rather than a body leaving a grave. On that reading the thousand years is a symbolic span covering the whole present age. A third reading takes the thousand years as a long figurative epoch of gospel flourishing within history, before the return. Second, the number itself, a thousand, can be a literal count or a symbol of fullness. Revelation elsewhere uses thousands in symbolic numerical schemes (1260 days, 144000, the seven sevens), and Peter uses the same words in an explicitly figurative way, both of which weigh toward symbolism. The Old Testament anchors describe a coming day when the LORD reigns as king over all the earth and a peaceable order where wolf and lamb lie down together, and one passage in Isaiah 65 mentions death still happening in that era, which is the strongest single text for an intervening era distinct from the final new creation. But none of these passages attaches a fixed length to the reign or dates it before or after any specific resurrection event. Because each reading is defensible from the words on the page and the text supplies no lexical hinge that settles the order or the duration, the honest finding is that the pattern is contested rather than plainly for or against.
